claims.evidence: Supported by FPKM values shown in Figure 1D

claims.claim: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation.
claims.source: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation (Figure 1E, left Heatmap), suggesting that high Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an OL-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of FPKM values in Figure 1E

claims.claim: High Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an oligodendrocyte-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
claims.source: FPKM values for Zdhhc9 and Golga7 were far lower in total RNA preps obtained from whole cortices without specific cell type isolation (Figure 1E, left Heatmap), suggesting that high Zdhhc9 and Golga7 expression is an OL-specific feature, rather than a general characteristic of CNS cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of FPKM values between OL-specific and whole cortex samples

claims.claim: Another CNS cell type-specific RNA-Seq dataset confirmed high and specific expression of Zdhhc9 and Golga7 in myelin-forming oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, examination of another CNS cell type-specific RNA-Seq dataset, obtained with sorted cells from P17 brain cortices via immunopanning (Zhang et al., 2014), confirmed high and specific expression of Zdhhc9 and Golga7 in myelin-forming OLs (Figure 1E, right Heatmap).
claims.evidence: Supported by data from Zhang et al., 2014 shown in Figure 1E

claims.claim: In human CNS, both ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 are enriched in oligodendrocytes, compared to any other PATs or other GOLGA family members.
claims.source: Moreover, examination of a human RNA-Seq study (Zhang et al., 2016) revealed that, like mouse CNS, both ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 are enriched in human OLs, compared to any other PATs or other GOLGA family members, respectively. (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by data from Zhang et al., 2016 shown in Figure 1F

claims.claim: HA-ZDHHC3, HA-ZDHHC7, and HA-ZDHHC17 were only detected in oligodendrocyte cell bodies.
claims.source: Under these conditions, HA-ZDHHC3, HA-ZDHHC7, and HA-ZDHHC17 were only detected in OL cell bodies, consistent with their restriction to the somatic Golgi in other cell types (Fang et al., 2006; Niu et al., 2020; Collura et al., 2020; Ohno et al., 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Figure 2B and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and D

claims.claim: HA-ZDHHC9 was detected both in oligodendrocyte cell bodies and in discrete puncta in oligodendrocyte processes.
claims.source: In contrast, HA-ZDHHC9 was detected both in OL cell bodies and in discrete puncta in OL processes (Figure 2B and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and D

claims.claim: Within oligodendrocyte cell bodies, ZDHHC9 partially colocalized with the Golgi marker GM130.
claims.source: Within OL cell bodies, ZDHHC9 partially colocalized with the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claims.claim: ZDHHC9 colocalized in part with additional Golgi markers (TGN38, Giantin).
claims.source: Consistent with this Golgi localization, ZDHHC9 also colocalized in part with additional Golgi markers (TGN38, Giantin; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claims.claim: Golgi markers GM130, TGN38, and Giantin were not detected in oligodendrocyte processes.
claims.source: However, these markers were not detected in OL processes and therefore did not colocalize with ZDHHC9 in this latter location (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D

claims.claim: XLID-associated HA-ZDHHC9 mutants (R96W, R148W, P150S) did not localize to oligodendrocyte processes.
claims.source: In contrast to HA-ZDHHC9WT, these XLID-associated HA-ZDHHC9 mutants did not localize to OL processes (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C and D

claims.claim: Myc-tagged Golga7 colocalized extensively with HA-ZDHHC9 in both oligodendrocyte cell bodies and in discrete puncta in oligodendrocyte processes.
claims.source: Consistent with this role, myc-tagged Golga7 (myc-Golga7) colocalized extensively with HA-ZDHHC9 in both OL cell bodies and in discrete puncta in OL processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claims.claim: ZDHHC9-positive puncta in oligodendrocyte processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP).
claims.source: Consistent with their assignation as Golgi outposts, ZDHHC9-positive puncta in OL processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP) and, to a lesser extent, with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claims.claim: ZDHHC9-positive puncta in oligodendrocyte processes colocalized to a lesser extent with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag).
claims.source: Consistent with their assignation as Golgi outposts, ZDHHC9-positive puncta in OL processes colocalized with GFP-tagged ManII (ManII-GFP) and, to a lesser extent, with Flag-tagged TPPP (TPPP-Flag) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claims.claim: There was no apparent difference in MBP-labeled oligodendrocyte processes between WT control and Zdhhc9 KO mice at 6 weeks of age.
claims.source: Histological observations of brain sections from 6-week-old male mice revealed no apparent difference in MBP-labeled OL processes between WT control and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte numbers in cortex and corpus callosum did not differ significantly between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: OL numbers in CTX and the corpus callosum (CC), assessed using OL markers aspartoacylase (ASPA) or Quaking 7 (recognized by antibody CC1), also did not detect any significant difference between the two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C

claims.claim: Preliminary analysis of the early oligodendrocyte marker BCAS1 did not reveal obvious differences between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: In addition, preliminary analysis of the early OL marker breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1 (BCAS1) did not reveal obvious differences between the two genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claims.claim: EGFP+ oligodendrocyte density did not differ significantly between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice in cortex, corpus callosum, and spinal cord at P28 and P56.
claims.source: Again, we did not detect significant differences in EGFP+ OL density between the two genotypes in three examined CNS regions (CTX, CC, and spinal cord), at two different ages (P28, P56; Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3B and C

claims.claim: The density of NG2+ OL progenitor cells did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: We also detected no difference in the density of NG2+ OL progenitor cells (OPCs) between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3D and E

claims.claim: There were no differences in the number of newly formed EGFP-labeled ASPA+ oligodendrocytes between control and Zdhhc9 KO mice in OPC fate tracing experiments.
claims.source: However, we did not detect differences in the number of newly formed EGFP-labeled ASPA+ OLs and % of EGFP+ OLs (Figure 3H, I) and the ratio of OLs to OPCs among EGFP-labeled cells (data not shown) between the two groups.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3H and I

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO does not alter oligodendrogenesis in either the young or mature CNS.
claims.source: These results suggest that Zdhhc9 KO does not alter oligodendrogenesis in either the young or mature CNS, at least using the markers and methodologies that we employed.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of differences in OL numbers and fate tracing results

claims.claim: The overall oligodendrocyte process complexity was slightly increased in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: Sholl analysis of these reconstructions revealed that the overall OL process complexity was slightly increased in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data in Figure 4C

claims.claim: The primary and secondary branch processes were longer in Zdhhc9 KO than control mice.
claims.source: More surprisingly, the primary and secondary branch process were longer in Zdhhc9 KO than control mice (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by process length quantification in Figure 4D

claims.claim: In control mice, the EGFP-labeled processes originating from one oligodendrocyte soma were of similar thickness, with a uniformly smooth structure.
claims.source: In control mice, the EGFP-labeled processes originating from one OL soma were of similar thickness, with a uniformly smooth structure.
claims.evidence: Based on observation of images in Figure 5A

claims.claim: The thickness of mEGFP+ processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice was far more heterogeneous, with several spheroid-like swellings.
claims.source: However, the thickness of mEGFP+ processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice was far more heterogeneous, with several spheroid-like swellings (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by images in Figure 5A and B

claims.claim: The abnormal spheroid-like swellings on oligodendrocyte processes were distinguished from oligodendrocyte somas as they lack signal for DAPI or Olig2.
claims.source: Notably, the abnormal spheroid-like swellings on OL processes were distinguished from OL somas as they lack signal for DAPI or Olig2 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO oligodendrocytes have significant structural abnormalities in their processes.
claims.source: Careful tracing of EGFP+ OL processes connected to DAPI+ cell body and quantification of spheroid-like swellings devoid of DAPI signal (Figure 5C-1, C-2) revealed significant structural abnormalities in OL processes in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5D and E

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 loss greatly alters the structure of individual oligodendrocyte processes at the microscopic level.
claims.source: These results indicate that, in contrast to its lack of effect at the gross level, Zdhhc9 loss greatly alters the structure of individual OL processes at the microscopic level, presumably due to abnormal OL membrane expansion.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the structural abnormalities observed in Figure 5

claims.claim: The number of axons did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice in P56 corpus callosum.
claims.source: In electron micrographs from P56 CC, the number of axons did not differ between WT and Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6A and B

claims.claim: Most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice.
claims.source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 6A

claims.claim: Myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal, with many large axons unmyelinated.
claims.source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification in Figure 6A and C

claims.claim: A subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appeared to be hypermyelinated in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: However, while most axons were evenly myelinated in WT mice, myelin patterns of axons in Zdhhc9 KO mice were highly abnormal; with many large axons unmyelinated (Figure 6A and C) and a subset of small diameter axons (<0.5 μm) appearing to be hypermyelinated (Figure 6A and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification in Figure 6A and D

claims.claim: G-ratios of small diameter axons were smaller in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the latter finding, g-ratios of these small diameter axons were smaller in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 6E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by g-ratio analysis in Figure 6E and F

claims.claim: At P30, both hypo- and hypermyelination of axons was already noticeable in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: However, in Zdhhc9 KO mice, both hypo- and hypermyelination of axons was already noticeable at this developmental stage (Figure 6G), which was evident from an increased interquartile range of g-ratios (Figure 6H, I).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and g-ratio analysis in Figure 6G, H, I

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination.
claims.source: These findings suggest that Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination and, thus, that ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the myelination deficits observed at P30 and P56

claims.claim: ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
claims.source: These findings suggest that Zdhhc9 loss results in dysmyelination and, thus, that ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the myelination deficits observed at P30 and P56

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes had significantly reduced expression of MBP, compared to oligodendrocytes infected to express a scrambled shRNA.
claims.source: Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs had significantly reduced expression of MBP, compared to OLs infected to express a scrambled shRNA (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 7B–D

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes still expressed CNP, an early myelin-specific protein of developing oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: However, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs still expressed 2',3'-Cyclic nucleotide 3'-phosphodiesterase (CNP), an early myelin-specific protein of developing OLs (Baumann and Pham-Dinh, 2001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: ZDHHC9 is not required for initial differentiation of OPCs to oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: This result suggests that ZDHHC9 is not required for initial differentiation of OPCs to OLs, consistent with the normal number of OLs seen in Zdhhc9 KO mice in vivo (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Inferred from CNP expression in Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs and normal OL numbers in KO mice

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes were morphologically immature.
claims.source: However, consistent with the reduced and restricted MBP expression, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs were also morphologically immature (Figure 7E) with a reduced degree of branching confirmed by Sholl analysis (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and Sholl analysis in Figure 7E and F

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 knockdown oligodendrocytes had a reduced degree of branching.
claims.source: However, consistent with the reduced and restricted MBP expression, Zdhhc9 knockdown OLs were also morphologically immature (Figure 7E) with a reduced degree of branching confirmed by Sholl analysis (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis in Figure 7F

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 loss cell-autonomously impairs oligodendrocyte maturation in vitro.
claims.source: These data indicate that Zdhhc9 loss cell-autonomously impairs OL maturation in vitro.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the effects of acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured OLs

claims.claim: Palmitoylation of 21.5 kDa MBP was very low when transfected alone.
claims.source: Palmitoylation of 21.5 kDa MBP (one of two MBP isoforms that contains a cysteine residue and is thus capable of undergoing palmitoylation) was very low when transfected alone.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: MBP palmitoylation remained very low when either HA-ZDHHC9 or myc-Golga7 were co-transfected in isolation.
claims.source: MBP palmitoylation remained very low when either HA-ZDHHC9 or myc-Golga7 were co-transfected in isolation (Figure 8A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: MBP palmitoylation was greatly increased by co-transfection of HA-ZDHHC9 and myc-Golga7.
claims.source: However, MBP palmitoylation was greatly increased by co-transfection of HA-ZDHHC9 and myc-Golga7 (Figure 8A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8A and B

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO did not affect total MBP levels measured by western blotting.
claims.source: Consistent with in vivo immunostaining results (Figure 3A), Zdhhc9 KO did not affect total MBP levels measured by western blotting (all isoforms assessed together; Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 8C and D

claims.claim: Palmitoylation of both the 17 kDa and 21.5 kDa MBP isoforms was significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: Importantly, palmitoylation, but not total expression, of both the 17 kDa and 21.5 kDa MBP isoforms was significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data from brain tissue in Figure 8C and D

claims.claim: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were also significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice, although the palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B

claims.claim: The palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not significantly affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: Total and palmitoyl- levels of MAG were also significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 KO mice, although the palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG was not (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B

claims.claim: Neither palmitoyl-, total, nor palmitoyl:total levels of Cadm4 were affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice.
claims.source: In the same samples, neither palmitoyl-, total, nor palmitoyl:total levels of Cadm4 were affected in Zdhhc9 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D

claims.claim: ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP with the support of Golga7.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP with the support of Golga7 and that Zdhhc9 loss impairs MBP palmitoylation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the ABE assay results in heterologous cells and brain tissue

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 loss impairs MBP palmitoylation.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP with the support of Golga7 and that Zdhhc9 loss impairs MBP palmitoylation.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data from Zdhhc9 KO brain tissue

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 loss impacts other myelin protein levels and/or regulation.
claims.source: In addition, Zdhhc9 loss impacts other myelin protein levels and/or regulation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the effects on MAG levels

claims.claim: MBP palmitoylation by the XLID mutant ZDHHC9-R148W is almost undetectable in cotransfected heterologous cells.
claims.source: We found that MBP palmitoylation by the XLID mutant ZDHHC9-R148W is almost undetectable in cotransfected heterologous cells and was minimally increased by additional cotransfection of Golga7.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8E and F

claims.claim: ZDHHC9-R96W palmitoylated MBP only approximately 50% as effectively as ZDHHC9wt in the presence of Golga7.
claims.source: Surprisingly, though, ZDHHC9-R96W palmitoylated MBP only approximately 50% as effectively as ZDHHC9wt in the presence of Golga7.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8E and F

claims.claim: ZDHHC9-P150S did not differ significantly from ZDHHC9wt in its ability to palmitoylate MBP in the presence of Golga7.
claims.source: Moreover, ZDHHC9-P150S did not differ significantly from ZDHHC9wt in its ability to palmitoylate MBP in the presence of Golga7.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8E and F

claims.claim: Autopalmitoylation of ZDHHC9wt and ZDHHC9-P150S did not differ significantly in the presence of Golga7.
claims.source: Moreover, autopalmitoylation (sometimes used as a surrogate marker of ZDHHC-PAT activity) of ZDHHC9wt and ZDHHC9-P150S also did not differ significantly in the presence of Golga7, suggesting that ZDHHC9-P150S may have sufficient catalytic activity to drive palmitoylation of an array of substrates.
claims.evidence: Supported by ABE assay data in Figure 8E and G

claims.claim: ZDHHC9-P150S may have sufficient catalytic activity to drive palmitoylation of an array of substrates.
claims.source: Moreover, autopalmitoylation (sometimes used as a surrogate marker of ZDHHC-PAT activity) of ZDHHC9wt and ZDHHC9-P150S also did not differ significantly in the presence of Golga7, suggesting that ZDHHC9-P150S may have sufficient catalytic activity to drive palmitoylation of an array of substrates.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the autopalmitoylation data

claims.claim: Dysregulated subcellular localization may be a more important factor than altered catalytic activity in certain cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.source: These findings further suggest that dysregulated subcellular localization may be a more important factor than altered catalytic activity in certain cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combination of localization and catalytic activity data for XLID mutants

claims.claim: Mobp-EGFP BAC transgenic mice express EGFP only in mature oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: To assess Zdhhc9 expression in OLs, we performed FACS using cerebral cortex (CTX) of P30 Mobp-EGFP BAC transgenic (Tg) mice, which express EGFP only in mature OLs (Figure 1A; Gong et al., 2003; Kang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature and confirmed by Figure 1A

claims.claim: Golgi outposts were recently reported to be present in oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Interestingly, Golgi outposts were also recently reported to be present in OLs (Fu et al., 2019), and a subset of OL Golgi outposts can be marked by the proteins TPPP and Mannosidase II (ManII) (Mikhaylova et al., 2016; Govind et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claims.claim: A subset of oligodendrocyte Golgi outposts can be marked by the proteins TPPP and Mannosidase II (ManII).
claims.source: Interestingly, Golgi outposts were also recently reported to be present in OLs (Fu et al., 2019), and a subset of OL Golgi outposts can be marked by the proteins TPPP and Mannosidase II (ManII) (Mikhaylova et al., 2016; Govind et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claims.claim: Patients with ZDHHC9 mutations have been diagnosed as young as two years of age based on behavioral milestones.
claims.source: Based on behavioral milestones, patients with ZDHHC9-associated XLID have been diagnosed as young as two years of age (Schirwani et al., 2018), suggesting that ZDHHC9 is important for higher brain function during early development.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior clinical study

claims.claim: P30 mice are approximately equivalent to a 3-year-old human.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, we observed dysmyelination (both hyper and hypomyelination) in P30 mice, approximately equivalent to a 3-year-old human (Dutta and Sengupta, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature on developmental equivalence

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have seizures, reminiscent of the rolandic epilepsy reported in many human patients with ZDHHC9 mutation.
claims.source: Most notably, Zdhhc9 KO mice have seizures, reminiscent of the rolandic epilepsy reported in many human patients with ZDHHC9 mutation (Baker et al., 2015; Shimell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have impaired latency to reach a hidden platform in the Morris Water Maze.
claims.source: Zdhhc9 KO mice also have impaired latency to reach a hidden platform in the Morris Water Maze (MWM), a task designed to assess spatial learning (Kouskou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice do not differ significantly in reference memory in a probe trial.
claims.source: However, the KO mice do not differ significantly in reference memory in a subsequent probe trial, suggesting that, despite the increased latency, they do learn the location of the platform as effectively as wt (Kouskou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice have decreased levels of anxiety.
claims.source: In addition, performance in both the open field and in an elevated plus maze (EPM, in which the KO mice spend significantly more time in the open arms) suggests that Zdhhc9 KO mice also have decreased levels of anxiety (Kouskou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claims.claim: Decreased anxiety is reported in several other mouse models of intellectual disability.
claims.source: Decreased anxiety is reported in several other mouse models of ID (Zang et al., 2009; Samaco et al., 2008; Escorihuela et al., 1998; Peier et al., 2000; Altafaj et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claims.claim: Zdhhc9 KO mice spend significantly less time on a hanging wire task.
claims.source: Finally, Zdhhc9 KO mice spend significantly less time on a hanging wire task (Kouskou et al., 2018), a phenotype consistent with hypotonia, a phenotype also reported in patients with ZDHHC9 mutation (Raymond et al., 2007; Masurel-Paulet et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claims.claim: Hypotonia is reported in patients with ZDHHC9 mutation.
claims.source: Finally, Zdhhc9 KO mice spend significantly less time on a hanging wire task (Kouskou et al., 2018), a phenotype consistent with hypotonia, a phenotype also reported in patients with ZDHHC9 mutation (Raymond et al., 2007; Masurel-Paulet et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies

claims.claim: Hypotonia is seen in several human neurodevelopmental conditions and relevant mouse models.
claims.source: Like reduced anxiety, hypotonia is seen in several human neurodevelopmental conditions and relevant mouse models (see Kouskou et al., 2018 and references therein for a fuller discussion).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claims.claim: XLID-associated mutant forms of ZDHHC9 show reduced protein stability.
claims.source: Moreover, XLID-associated mutant forms of ZDHHC9 also show reduced protein stability and are impaired in their ability to form complexes with Golga7 (also known as Golgi Complex Protein 16 kDa; GCP16)(Nguyen et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claims.claim: XLID-associated mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are impaired in their ability to form complexes with Golga7.
claims.source: Moreover, XLID-associated mutant forms of ZDHHC9 also show reduced protein stability and are impaired in their ability to form complexes with Golga7 (also known as Golgi Complex Protein 16 kDa; GCP16)(Nguyen et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claims.claim: Impaired palmitoylation of MBP, and potentially other myelin proteins, in the absence of ZDHHC9 affects myelin structure.
claims.source: Given that palmitoylation can sort proteins to the myelin membrane (Schneider et al., 2005), the simplest explanation might be that impaired palmitoylation of MBP, and potentially other myelin proteins, in the absence of ZDHHC9 affects myelin structure per se.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on known role of palmitoylation and observed myelin deficits

claims.claim: ZDHHC9 may act at Golgi outposts to drive the expression of myelin protein genes.
claims.source: Another non-mutually exclusive possibility is that ZDHHC9 acts at Golgi outposts but indirectly, for example, to drive the expression of myelin protein genes.
claims.evidence: Speculative possibility discussed by authors

claims.claim: The association with Golga7 is central to ZDHHC9 activity.
claims.source: Interestingly, despite their marked differences in basal catalytic activity (as assessed by autopalmitoylation), wt and all XLID forms of ZDHHC9 appear to show enhanced activity (measured by both auto- and MBP palmitoylation) in the presence of Golga7, suggesting that the association with Golga7 (which also localizes to Golgi outposts) is central to ZDHHC9 activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the enhancement of ZDHHC9 activity by Golga7 in ABE assays

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte and white matter abnormalities could significantly contribute to ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.source: Together, though, our findings suggest that OL and WM abnormalities could significantly contribute to ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the OL and myelin deficits observed in Zdhhc9 KO mice

claims.claim: Impaired subcellular localization in oligodendrocytes, rather than impaired catalytic activity, may cause or contribute to white matter abnormalities in some cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.source: Interestingly, the XLID mutant ZDHHC9-P150S still palmitoylates MBP in a Golga7-dependent manner in transfected non-neuronal cells, raising the possibility that impaired subcellular localization in OLs, rather than impaired catalytic activity, may cause or contribute to WM abnormalities in some cases of ZDHHC9-associated XLID.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the retained catalytic activity but impaired localization of ZDHHC9-P150S

results.result: ZDHHC9 and its partner GOLGA7 are highly and specifically expressed in oligodendrocytes in both mouse and human CNS, with ZDHHC9 being the most highly expressed PAT in these cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C32-C42 collectively demonstrate oligodendrocyte-specific enrichment of ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 through multiple independent RNA-seq datasets (authors' own data, Zhang et al. 2014, Zhang et al. 2016) in both mouse and human tissue. The FPKM values, heatmaps, and cross-validation across datasets provide strong converging evidence.

results.result: Wild-type ZDHHC9 uniquely localizes to Golgi outposts in oligodendrocyte processes, whereas other PATs and XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C43-C51 are supported by immunofluorescence data in cultured oligodendrocytes (Figure 2 and supplements) showing differential localization patterns. The colocalization with Golgi outpost markers (ManII, TPPP) and partner protein Golga7 provides additional validation. Quantification in Figure 2D confirms statistical significance.

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout mice have grossly normal oligodendrocyte development with no significant changes in oligodendrocyte or OPC numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C52-C58 are supported by multiple quantification approaches (MBP staining, ASPA/CC1 markers, EGFP+ cell counts, NG2+ OPC counts, fate tracing) across multiple CNS regions and developmental timepoints (Figure 3 and supplements). Statistical analyses show no significant differences between genotypes.

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout oligodendrocytes display extensive microscale morphological abnormalities including heterogeneous process thickness and spheroid-like swellings, despite slightly increased overall process complexity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by sparse genetic labeling, 3D reconstruction, and Sholl analysis (Figure 4-5). The spheroid-like swellings are distinguished from cell bodies by absence of DAPI/Olig2 signal and are quantified showing significant differences (Figure 5D-E, p<0.001).

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout mice exhibit dysmyelination with both hypomyelination of large axons and hypermyelination of small axons, evident at both P30 and P56.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 are supported by electron microscopy and g-ratio analysis at two developmental timepoints (Figure 6). The presence of deficits at P30 (during active myelination) supports the conclusion that this represents dysmyelination rather than demyelination. Statistical significance is demonstrated for multiple parameters.

results.result: Acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured oligodendrocytes cell-autonomously impairs oligodendrocyte maturation, reducing MBP expression and morphological complexity while preserving CNP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C74-C79 are supported by lentiviral shRNA knockdown experiments in cultured OLs (Figure 7). The retention of CNP expression but loss of MBP and reduced branching complexity (Sholl analysis) indicates impaired maturation rather than failed differentiation. Statistical significance is shown for multiple parameters.

results.result: ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP in a Golga7-dependent manner in heterologous cells, and MBP palmitoylation is significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 knockout brain tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C80-C84, C88-C89 are supported by ABE assays in both HEK293T cells (Figure 8A-B) and brain white matter tissue (Figure 8C-D). The requirement for both ZDHHC9 and Golga7 for robust MBP palmitoylation in cells, and the significant reduction in palmitoyl-MBP (but not total MBP) in KO brain provide strong evidence.

results.result: XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 show variable catalytic activity, with P150S retaining near-normal MBP palmitoylation activity, suggesting that impaired subcellular localization may be more important than catalytic deficiency in some XLID cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by ABE assays comparing wild-type and mutant ZDHHC9 forms (Figure 8E-G). The finding that P150S shows normal autopalmitoylation and MBP palmitoylation despite failing to localize to OL processes (Figure 2C-D) supports the conclusion about localization versus catalytic activity, though this remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Zdhhc9 loss reduces total and palmitoyl-MAG levels but does not affect the palmitoyl:total ratio of MAG or any Cadm4 measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87, C90 are supported by ABE assays on brain white matter tissue (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The selective effect on MAG but not Cadm4 suggests specificity rather than global myelin protein dysregulation, though the mechanism for MAG reduction remains unclear.

results.result: ZDHHC9 mutations cause X-linked intellectual disability with epilepsy in humans, and patients show reduced white matter volume; Zdhhc9 knockout mice recapitulate key phenotypes including white matter reductions and seizures.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C23 are supported by citations to prior clinical and mouse model literature. These claims establish the clinical and translational context for the study but represent prior work rather than new findings from this manuscript.

results.result: ZDHHC9 encodes a protein acyltransferase that palmitoylates proteins including major myelin proteins, and ZDHHC9 requires Golga7 as a partner protein for activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31, C37 represent established background knowledge supported by citations to prior literature. These provide essential context but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: Various methodological validations and contextual information from prior studies including mouse model characterization, Golgi outpost markers, developmental timing equivalence, and behavioral phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C111 are supported by citations to prior literature and provide methodological validation and contextual information. These are important for interpreting the main findings but represent supporting rather than primary results.

results.result: The authors propose that impaired MBP palmitoylation affects myelin structure, that ZDHHC9 may regulate myelin protein gene expression at Golgi outposts, that Golga7 association is central to ZDHHC9 activity, and that oligodendrocyte/white matter abnormalities contribute to XLID.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 represent speculative interpretations and mechanistic hypotheses discussed by the authors. While these are reasonable inferences from the data, they are explicitly speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., conditional knockout, rescue experiments, mechanistic studies of Golgi outpost function) to be definitively supported.

results.result: ZDHHC9 and its partner Golga7 are highly and specifically expressed in myelinating oligodendrocytes compared to other CNS cell types, as demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of FACS-isolated oligodendrocytes from mouse and examination of human CNS datasets. ZDHHC9 is the most highly expressed PAT in oligodendrocytes with FPKM ~180.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding, with one stating the study 'provides an in-depth exploration...with a particular focus on the expression and function of ZDHHC9 in myelin-forming oligodendrocytes' and noting 'good data quality.' The anonymous reviewer confirmed the authors 'having shown that acyltransferase ZDHHC9 expression is far higher in myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs) than in other CNS cell types.' No concerns were raised about the RNA-seq data or expression analysis.

results.result: Wild-type ZDHHC9 uniquely localizes to Golgi outposts in oligodendrocyte processes, while other PATs (ZDHHC3, ZDHHC7, ZDHHC17) and XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 are restricted to cell bodies. ZDHHC9 colocalizes with its partner Golga7 and Golgi outpost markers ManII and TPPP in oligodendrocyte processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these localization findings without challenge. The editor noted 'the experimental design and analysis of results are solid,' and the anonymous reviewer stated the 'use of transgenics strategies (in addition to the ZDHHC9 KO) strengthen the data and claims.' The immunofluorescence data showing differential localization of ZDHHC9 versus other PATs and mutant forms was not questioned.

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout mice have grossly normal oligodendrocyte development with no significant differences in oligodendrocyte numbers, OPC density, or oligodendrogenesis as assessed by multiple markers (MBP, ASPA, CC1, BCAS1, NG2) and fate tracing experiments at multiple developmental timepoints.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings about normal oligodendrocyte development. The editor praised the 'solid' experimental design, and the anonymous reviewer noted 'in general good data quality.' The comprehensive quantification across multiple markers, timepoints, and CNS regions was accepted without requests for additional validation.

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout mice display extensive morphological abnormalities in oligodendrocyte processes, including increased process complexity and length, heterogeneous process thickness with spheroid-like swellings, indicating altered structure at the microscopic level despite grossly normal appearance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these morphological findings. The editor stated the results 'provide insights into ZDHHC9-related X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) and shed light on the regulatory mechanisms of palmitoylation in myelination.' The anonymous reviewer acknowledged the study 'provides useful insights the mechanisms of ZDHHC9-associated XLID' without questioning the morphological analysis or sparse labeling data.

results.result: Zdhhc9 knockout mice exhibit severe dysmyelination with both hypomyelination of large axons and hypermyelination of small diameter axons, evident at both P30 and P56, indicating ZDHHC9 is required for proper initial myelination of individual axons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the electron microscopy findings or dysmyelination phenotype. The editor noted the findings 'offer insights into ZDHHC9-related X-linked intellectual disability,' and the anonymous reviewer stated the study 'provides useful insights...on the palmitoylation-dependent control of myelination.' The g-ratio analysis and quantification of myelination defects were accepted without critique.

results.result: Acute Zdhhc9 knockdown in cultured oligodendrocytes phenocopies in vivo deficits, showing reduced MBP expression, morphological immaturity, and reduced branching, while maintaining CNP expression, indicating cell-autonomous impairment of oligodendrocyte maturation without affecting initial differentiation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the cultured oligodendrocyte data as supporting evidence for cell-autonomous effects. The anonymous reviewer specifically noted that 'use of transgenics strategies (in addition to the ZDHHC9 KO) strengthen the data and claims,' implicitly endorsing the complementary in vitro approach. No concerns were raised about the shRNA knockdown experiments or interpretation.

results.result: ZDHHC9 directly palmitoylates MBP in a Golga7-dependent manner in heterologous cells, and palmitoylation of both 17 kDa and 21.5 kDa MBP isoforms is significantly reduced in Zdhhc9 knockout brain tissue without affecting total MBP levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the palmitoylation findings. The editor stated the study 'shed[s] light on the regulatory mechanisms of palmitoylation in myelination,' and the anonymous reviewer noted the study 'provides useful insights...on the palmitoylation-dependent control of myelination.' The ABE assay data from both heterologous cells and brain tissue was not questioned.

results.result: Zdhhc9 loss affects other myelin proteins beyond MBP, with reduced total and palmitoylated MAG levels (though palmitoyl:total ratio unchanged), while Cadm4 levels remain unaffected, indicating selective effects on myelin protein regulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings about effects on other myelin proteins. The data on MAG and Cadm4 were presented as supplementary evidence and accepted without critique. The anonymous reviewer's general statement about 'good data quality' encompasses these biochemical analyses.

results.result: XLID mutant forms of ZDHHC9 show differential effects: R148W has almost undetectable MBP palmitoylation activity, R96W shows ~50% activity, while P150S retains full catalytic activity comparable to wild-type, suggesting dysregulated subcellular localization may be more important than catalytic activity in certain XLID cases.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not explicitly challenge these findings, the anonymous reviewer noted 'a few claims might have needed better experimental support but new data and revised discussion sections addressed some of these weaknesses.' This suggests some initial uncertainty about mechanistic interpretations that was partially resolved through revision. The speculative nature of the localization versus catalytic activity hypothesis (C96) remains somewhat uncertain despite the supporting data.

results.result: Background context establishing that ZDHHC9 mutations cause X-linked intellectual disability with epilepsy in humans, that patients show white matter abnormalities, and that Zdhhc9 knockout mice recapitulate key phenotypes including white matter volume reductions and seizures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this background context without challenge. The editor noted the study 'provides an in-depth exploration of the impact of X-linked ZDHHC9 gene mutations on cognitive deficits and epilepsy,' affirming the clinical relevance. These citation-based claims about prior literature were not questioned.

results.result: The authors conclude that oligodendrocyte and white matter abnormalities could significantly contribute to ZDHHC9-associated XLID, and that impaired subcellular localization rather than catalytic activity may cause white matter abnormalities in some cases.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretive conclusions. The anonymous reviewer stated the study 'suggests a more relevant role for myelinating glia than previously thought' and 'provides useful insights the mechanisms of ZDHHC9-associated XLID,' directly endorsing the authors' conclusions about oligodendrocyte contributions to intellectual disability. The editor similarly noted the findings 'offer insights into ZDHHC9-related X-linked intellectual disability.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on oligodendrocyte-specific enrichment of ZDHHC9 and GOLGA7 (C3, C4, C32-C42). Both evaluations find the RNA-seq data across multiple datasets strongly supportive. Peer reviewers explicitly praised 'good data quality' and the comprehensive expression analysis.

Complete agreement on localization findings (C5-C7, C43-C51). Both evaluations accept the immunofluorescence data showing differential localization patterns. Peer reviewers noted the transgenic strategies 'strengthen the data and claims' without raising concerns about the localization evidence.

Full concordance on normal oligodendrocyte development findings (C8, C52-C58). Both evaluations find the comprehensive quantification across markers, timepoints, and CNS regions convincing. Peer reviewers accepted this without requesting additional validation.

Strong agreement on morphological abnormalities (C59-C65), though peer review also includes C9. Both evaluations accept the sparse labeling, 3D reconstruction, and Sholl analysis data. Peer reviewers acknowledged the study provides useful insights into XLID mechanisms without challenging the morphological findings.

Complete agreement on dysmyelination phenotype (C66-C73). Both evaluations find the electron microscopy and g-ratio analysis convincing. Peer reviewers accepted the distinction between dysmyelination and demyelination without critique.

Full concordance on cultured oligodendrocyte findings (C10, C74-C79). Both evaluations accept the shRNA knockdown data as supporting cell-autonomous effects. Peer reviewers implicitly endorsed this complementary in vitro approach through their statement about transgenic strategies strengthening claims.

Perfect agreement on MBP palmitoylation findings (C11-C12, C80-C84, C88-C89). Both evaluations find the ABE assay data from heterologous cells and brain tissue strongly supportive. Peer reviewers explicitly noted the study sheds light on palmitoylation mechanisms in myelination.

Complete agreement on selective effects on MAG (C85-C87, C90). Both evaluations accept these findings about other myelin proteins. Peer reviewers' general statement about 'good data quality' encompasses these biochemical analyses without specific concerns.

Partial agreement on mutant ZDHHC9 analysis (C91-C96). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED while acknowledging speculation about localization versus catalytic activity. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, noting 'a few claims might have needed better experimental support' that was partially addressed through revision. Both recognize the speculative nature of mechanistic interpretations.

Full concordance on background/clinical context claims (C1-C2, C13-C23). Both evaluations accept these citation-based claims about prior literature establishing clinical relevance. Peer reviewers affirmed the study's connection to XLID without questioning the background.

Divergent evaluations of speculative interpretations. OpenEval rates C112-C116 as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing these are speculative hypotheses requiring additional experiments. Peer review rates only C115-C116 as SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing the authors' conclusions about oligodendrocyte contributions to intellectual disability. OpenEval is more conservative about mechanistic speculation.

OpenEval identified background knowledge claims (C24-C31, C37) as a distinct supported category representing established context from prior literature. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these background claims, likely incorporating them into their overall assessment of the study's foundation.

OpenEval identified methodological validation and contextual claims (C97-C111) as supported by prior literature. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these supporting methodological claims, though their acceptance of the overall experimental design implicitly endorses the methodological foundation.
